To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

preschoolers and adults represent pretense behavior in terms of contrasts between pretence and its real counterpart, but preschoolers place greater weight on deviance in content than on deviance in behavior, whereas adults use behavior, especially movement, as a cue to pretence when content information is not available.
5-year-olds and adults use different cues to judge whether an act is a pretense one, but both use the same basic principle to guide their judgments.

preschoolers and adults represent pretense behavior in a similar way, but preschoolers place greater weight on content cues than on behavioral cues when judging an act as a pretense or a real act, whereas adults use behavioral cues more than content cues.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of children’s understanding of pretense.
the nature of pretense.
the question of what makes an action a pretense one, and we have been studying this question by examining the judgments that adults and children make about the pretense or reality of an action.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
children’s pretense is more like adults’ than not, but that children’s pretenses are more limited in scope and less sophisticated in nature.
the children’s judgments and explanations of pretense are similar to those of adults, but that children place a greater weight on the content of pretense acts than on behavioral cues.
the children’s intuitive theories are not the same as those of adults.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the more children know about pretense, the more they use behavioral cues in their pretense judgments.
children’s intuitive theory of pretense is not a simple theory of pretense, but a theory of pretense that is not yet complete.
children’s and adults’ judgments and explanations of pretense are guided by the same underlying principles but that children’s judgments and explanations are not as sophisticated as those of adults.

preschoolers’ intuitive theories of pretence differ from those of adult in important ways.
